examples.problem_statement: Ernest Hemingway, the novelist and proponent of traditional masculine virtues that were already considered (i) _________ by his more progressive peers, eventually lost currency with the general public; although his earlier literary works remained popular, his continuing adherence to that code drove him to disdain society, which, in turn, (ii) _________ him. Blank (i) choices: effeminate, anachronistic, sardonic. Blank (ii) choices: shunned, eulogized, murdered.

solution.operation: Locate the clue governing blank (i): the judgment of his "more progressive peers" on virtues described as "traditional"
solution.result: Blank (i) must state how forward-looking people regard something traditional
solution.description: Read the blank against the words the sentence supplies about who is judging and what is being judged, so the blank is filled from the sentence's own evidence rather than from a guess.

solution.operation: Unpack "progressive" as wanting to move forward, away from traditions
solution.result: The needed word must brand the virtues as belonging to an earlier time
solution.description: Convert the clue word into the meaning it forces on the blank; progressive peers would fault traditional virtues for being out of their era.

solution.operation: Match that requirement to "anachronistic," meaning "in the wrong time period"
solution.result: Blank (i) = anachronistic
solution.description: Select the choice whose definition is exactly the out-of-its-time meaning the clue demands.

solution.operation: Read the pivot "in turn" joining his disdain for society to society's response
solution.result: Blank (ii) must reciprocate the disdain, that is, get him back for it
solution.description: Use the transition phrase to fix the direction of the second blank: it mirrors, rather than reverses, the action just described.

solution.operation: Pick the blank (ii) choice that matches disdain returned
solution.result: Blank (ii) = shunned
solution.description: Choose the word that carries the same disdainful charge back toward Hemingway, completing the reciprocal pair.

key_reminders: "Progressive" signals a move away from tradition, so it dates whatever is traditional.
"In turn" marks reciprocation: the second blank repeats the direction of the first action, not its opposite.
common_mistakes: Choosing "effeminate" by reacting to "masculine virtues" instead of to the progressive-versus-traditional time clue.
Choosing "eulogized" for blank (ii), which reverses the direction that "in turn" after "disdain" requires.

examples.problem_statement: Compare Quantity A and Quantity B. Set A consists of 40 integers, and set B consists of 150 integers. The number of integers that are in both set A and set B is 20. Quantity A: The total number of integers that are in set A or set B, or both. Quantity B: 170. (A) Quantity A is greater. (B) Quantity B is greater. (C) The two quantities are equal. (D) The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

solution.result: The three given counts are recorded
solution.description: Write down what the problem supplies before comparing anything, since the comparison is built entirely from these three counts.

solution.operation: Draw a Venn diagram of two overlapping circles labeled 40 and 150 with 20 in the overlap
solution.result: A picture in which the 20 shared integers sit inside both the 40 and the 150
solution.description: Translate the words into a figure; the diagram makes visible that the shared integers have been counted inside each circle's total.

solution.operation: Redraw with three separate regions: A only = 40 - 20, both = 20, B only = 150 - 20
solution.result: 20 in A only, 20 in both, 130 in B only
solution.description: Split the diagram so each integer is counted exactly once, which is what a total of A or B or both requires.
Add the three disjoint regions to get the total number of integers that are in set A or set B or both.

solution.operation: n(A) + n(B) - n(A \text{ and } B) = 40 + 150 - 20
solution.description: Check the same total the second way the book gives: listing both sets counts the shared integers twice, so subtract the overlap once.

solution.operation: Compare Quantity A = 170 with Quantity B = 170
solution.result: The two quantities are equal
solution.description: Set the computed union count against the given 170 and read off the comparison the question asks for.

examples.answer: Choice C: The two quantities are equal.

key_reminders: The count of a union is n(A) + n(B) - n(A \text{ and } B); the overlap is subtracted once because it was counted twice.
In a two-circle Venn diagram the given circle totals already include the overlap, so subtract it out before adding regions.
common_mistakes: Adding 40 + 150 to get 190 and calling Quantity A greater, forgetting that the 20 shared integers were counted twice.
Reading the circle labels 40 and 150 as the counts of A only and B only, which makes the regions 40, 20, and 150.

concept.technique_name: part-to-whole comparison by ratio estimation from a bar chart

examples.problem_statement: Using the column chart of monthly fruit and vegetable sales, which month had the greatest percentage of vegetable sales relative to total sales? (A) Jan (B) Mar (C) Jun (D) Oct (E) Nov

solution.operation: Recast "greatest percentage of vegetable sales relative to total sales" as "greatest ratio of vegetable sales to fruit sales"
solution.result: The task becomes a ratio comparison, not a percent computation
solution.description: Because total sales are only fruit plus vegetables, whichever month has vegetables largest against fruit also has them largest against the total.

solution.operation: Restrict attention to the five months named in the answer choices
solution.result: Only Jan, Mar, Jun, Oct, and Nov need to be examined
solution.description: Glance at the choices first so the chart is scanned for five columns instead of twelve.

solution.operation: Check Jan and Mar: vegetable bar above fruit bar
solution.result: In both months vegetables are more than half of total sales
solution.description: Compare the two bars within each month to see which side of one-half the vegetable share falls on.

solution.operation: Check Jun: fruit bar above vegetable bar
solution.result: Vegetables are less than half of total sales, so eliminate (C)
solution.description: A month where vegetables trail fruit cannot beat a month where they lead, so June is discarded.

solution.operation: Check Oct and Nov: fruit and vegetable bars about equal
solution.result: Vegetable share is about half, so eliminate (D) and (E)
solution.description: Near-equal bars give roughly a one-half share, which loses to Jan and Mar; only Jan and Mar remain.

solution.operation: Read the values: Jan vegetables \approx 2200, fruit \approx 1700; Mar vegetables \approx 2400, fruit \approx 2000
solution.result: January differential \approx 500 on a smaller total; March differential \approx 400 on a larger total
solution.description: The two survivors are close, so take approximate amounts off the chart and form the gap and the total for each month.

solution.operation: Compare a larger vegetable-over-fruit gap on a smaller total against a smaller gap on a larger total
solution.result: January's vegetable sales are the greater share of that month's total
solution.description: A bigger surplus spread over a smaller total is necessarily a bigger fraction of it, which settles January over March conceptually.

solution.operation: Confirm with the calculator by dividing each month's vegetable sales by that month's total
solution.result: January's percentage is slightly greater than March's
solution.description: Run the arithmetic check the book offers as the alternative to the conceptual comparison, confirming January.

key_reminders: With only two categories in a column, vegetables exceeding fruit is the same as vegetables exceeding half the total.
Scan the answer choices before the chart so only the listed months are read.
A larger surplus over a smaller total gives the larger share.
common_mistakes: Picking March because its vegetable bar is the tallest in absolute terms, when the question asks for a share of that month's total.
Treating Oct and Nov's roughly equal bars as a tie for the top instead of recognizing a share of about one-half.

concept.technique_name: charge and direction matching across answer choices

examples.problem_statement: Select the two answer choices that, when used to complete the sentence, fit the meaning of the sentence as a whole and produce completed sentences that are alike in meaning. Some of the company's supporters charged that the negative report had been motivated by a broader political assault on the company that was designed to help market rivals who would like to see the company ______ . (A) reined in (B) bolstered (C) indemnified (D) propped up (E) manacled (F) lionized

solution.operation: Identify whose wish the blank expresses: the company's "market rivals"
solution.result: The blank states what competitors want to happen to the company
solution.description: Anchor the blank to the party named right before it, since the sentence makes their preference the thing being described.

solution.operation: Fix the direction rivals would want
solution.result: Market rivals would clearly like to see the company experience some negative outcome
solution.description: Reason from who the rivals are to the charge of the missing word, so the choices can be sorted before any of them are weighed individually.

solution.operation: Sort the choices by charge: bolstered, indemnified, propped up, and lionized all describe positive results for the company
solution.result: Choices B, C, D, and F are eliminated
solution.description: Discard every option that would benefit the company, because none of them matches the negative direction the sentence requires.

solution.operation: Keep the choices that describe a negative outcome: reined in and manacled
solution.result: Only these two describe such an outcome
solution.description: The remaining pair both mean restrained or held back, which is the negative sense the rivals would welcome.

solution.operation: Confirm the surviving pair produces two sentences alike in meaning
solution.result: Reined in (Choice A) and manacled (Choice E)
solution.description: Sentence equivalence needs a matched pair, and these two restraint words satisfy that requirement together.

examples.answer: Choice A: reined in AND Choice E: manacled

key_reminders: Sorting the six choices by positive or negative charge usually removes most of them at once.
The blank must express what the named party, here the market rivals, would want.
The two selected words must yield sentences alike in meaning, so they come as a synonym pair.
common_mistakes: Pairing bolstered with propped up because they are synonyms of each other, ignoring that they give the company a positive outcome.
Choosing indemnified for its legal ring in a sentence about a negative report, though it protects rather than harms the company.
